```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

The classic use case of spring-phenology is model to have a single calibrated model for
each cultivar or phenological stage (budbreak, flowering). However,
there are situations where specialized model calibration may be desired. This vignette will demonstate evalphenos function to do cross-validation, the model calibration of several successive phenological stages and the partial pooling of model structure across cultivars.

In the first step, the phenology model is defined. In addition, the temperature data is converted to hourly format and split by season, meaning that we create a list with seperate
data.frames, each entry contains hourly temperature from the start of the season, by default September, to the end of the season, by default June in the following year. 

```{r weather}
library(evalpheno)

data("cka_weather", package = "evalpheno")
head(cka_weather)

hourly <- chillR::stack_hourly_temps(
  cka_weather, latitude = attr(cka_weather, "latitude")
)$hourtemps
years <- 2008:2009
seasons <- chillR::genSeasonList(hourly, mrange = c(8, 6), years = years)
names(seasons) <- as.character(years)
season <- seasons[[1]]


phenoflex_model <- pheno_model(structure = "phenoflex")
```

## Cross-validation and weighted mean predictions

Cross-validation can be usefull when we want to assess the uncertainty of the calibrated model parameters. Prepare the splits before fitting so they can be inspected. Each cross-validation fold retains a different set of training data for validation. In this example we have only two seasons, which is definitely not enough for real-world applications. Normally, 20 seasons or more are required for model training. The obtained models can also be used together to perform weighted mean predictions, as done for example by @caspersen_contrasting_2025.

```{r cross-validation}

observed <- c(`2008` = 125, `2009` = 117)

bounds <- default_bounds(phenoflex_model, parameter_names = c("yc", "zc"))
bounds$lower["zc"] <- 180
bounds$upper["zc"] <- 350

prepared <- prepare_phenology_cv(
  seasons, observed, years = years, v = 2, repeats = 1, seed = 21
)
prepared$assignments
cv <- fit_phenology_cv(
  phenoflex_model, data = prepared, evaluation = phenology_rss,
  lower = bounds$lower["zc"], upper = bounds$upper["zc"],
  optimizer = "DEoptim", max_iterations = 2,
  control = list(NP = 10, trace = FALSE),
  restarts = 1, refit = FALSE, weighting = "inverse_mse", seed = 22
)
cv$calibration$scores
cv$predictions # held-out predictions of each fold model
```

`repeats` redraws fold assignments; `restarts` repeats optimization within each
split and selects the lowest training loss. Only `zc` is fitted in this small
CV example. With sufficient data, use `groups = years` to keep entries of the
same year together, and reserve independent validation through
`validation_indices` or `validation_prop` before fitting.

Fold scores assess individual held-out predictions. An ensemble prediction on
these same seasons includes models trained on them and is **not** an independent
validation result. With a larger dataset and reserved entries, use
`validate_phenology(cv)` after choosing the ensemble policy. Ensemble spread is
descriptive, not a confidence interval; missing-event votes can suppress the
mean according to `failure_threshold`.

The CV result stores an ensemble of fold models. `"inverse_mse"` weights them
by `1 / (assessment MSE + epsilon)`; `"equal"` gives equal weights. Examine the
weights and predict with the weighted mean:

```{r weighted-predictions}
cv$model$weights
predict_phenology(cv, season)
weighted <- predict_phenology(cv, season, basic_output = FALSE)
weighted$summary
```

You can also set explicit weights for the same fold models:

```{r explicit-weights}
ensemble <- pheno_ensemble(cv, weights = c(0.4, 0.6))
predict_phenology(ensemble, season)
```



## Fit successive stages together

`stage_pheno_models()` uses ordered cumulative heat thresholds for successive
stages. This can be helpfull to model successive phenological stages such as budbreak, first flowering and full flowering [@caspersen_spring_2025] Heat does not restart at each stage. The ordering of stages is separate
from the choice of model structure; here the underlying structure is PhenoFlex.
All parameters except `zc1`, `zc2`, etc. are shared.

```{r stage-fit}
stages <- stage_pheno_models(
  phenoflex_model, c(budbreak = 180, first_bloom = 250, full_bloom = 300)
)
stage_observed <- list(
  budbreak = c(115, 105),
  first_bloom = c(125, 117),
  full_bloom = c(131, 123)
)
stage_fit <- fit_phenology(
  stages, evaluation = phenology_rss_stages,
  seasons = seasons, observed = stage_observed,
  lower = c(zc1 = 120, zc2 = 220, zc3 = 280),
  upper = c(zc1 = 220, zc2 = 280, zc3 = 350),
  max_iterations = 2, control = list(NP = 30, trace = FALSE), seed = 19
)
stage_fit$par[c("zc1", "zc2", "zc3")]
predict_phenology(stage_fit, seasons)
```

##  Fit cultivars together

Partially pooling observations from several cultivars can be usefull if each cultivar by
themselve does not have observation for a regular model calibration. You choose
which parameters of the models are shared across cultivars and which are cultivar-specific. For example, the submodels for chill and heat accumulation can be shared accross cultivars but the chill and heat requirements remain cultivar-specific. This approach was
developed by @caspersen_combining_2026.

For combined fitting, choose cultivar-specific structure parameters. All other
parameters are shared. Data are nested by cultivar, then season, and their
order must agree with the cultivar indices in the parameter names.

```{r combined-fit}
combined <- combined_pheno_model(
  phenoflex_model, n_cultivars = 2, cultivar_specific = c("yc", "zc")
)
combined_parameters <- model_parameters(combined)
combined_parameters[c("yc1", "yc2")] <- c(35, 45)
combined <- combined_pheno_model(
  phenoflex_model, n_cultivars = 2, cultivar_specific = c("yc", "zc"),
  parameters = combined_parameters
)
combined_seasons <- list(cultivar_a = seasons, cultivar_b = seasons)
combined_observed <- list(cultivar_a = observed, cultivar_b = c(130, 123))
combined_bounds <- default_bounds(combined, c("zc", "tau"))
combined_fit <- fit_phenology(
  combined, evaluation = phenology_rss_combined,
  seasons = combined_seasons, observed = combined_observed,
  lower = combined_bounds$lower, upper = combined_bounds$upper,
  max_iterations = 2, control = list(NP = 30, trace = FALSE), seed = 20
)
combined_fit$par[c("yc1", "yc2", "zc1", "zc2", "tau")]
predict_phenology(combined_fit, combined_seasons)
```

Here `yc1` and `yc2` are cultivar-specific but fixed. `zc1` and `zc2` are fitted
separately, and `tau` is fitted once for the shared chill submodel. Include
`"yc"` in `default_bounds()` to fit both chill requirements too. Shared heat
parameters can likewise be added to the search.
